tier_reason: Peer-reviewed artifact of the Bioinformatics 2023 BiWFA paper (smarco/BiWFA-paper evaluation/1_RealData.md scripts, tools/align_benchmark wrappers, evaluation/data/statistics_all.tsv.gz) with compiler (gcc 10.2.0) and flags (-O3 -march=native) stated; the CPU model is not stated in the repo and the paper (NCBI, bioRxiv, NSF PAR) was unreachable, so not A. I re-derived every ratio in claimed_speedup from the raw per-pair time_ms rows and they match.

corrections.hardware: BSC cluster jobs (the evaluation scripts copy data to amdlogin.bsc.es, BSC's AMD partition) submitted with sbatch -c 128 --exclusive, one alignment at a time per job loop; CPU model not stated in the repo.
corrections.caveats: The measured code is the BiWFA-paper snapshot (benchmark branch commit d5532da), not the current WFA2-lib main, and the data are long noisy reads at small divergence where WFA's O(ns) behaviour is most favourable; short reads or highly divergent pairs will show other ratios. CPU model is missing, so tier B (peer-reviewed artifact of the Bioinformatics 2023 BiWFA paper) not A; the paper itself was not reachable (NCBI, bioRxiv and NSF PAR blocked). The time_ms column is align_benchmark's own per-pair timer (InfoAlignment line parsed by evaluation/scripts/log2info.py): timer_start/timer_stop wrap only the alignment call in each wrapper (ksw_extz2_sse for ksw2), the --check correct verification runs outside the timer, and --repeat 100000 is a target number of aligned bases, so long pairs run once and shorter pairs are averaged over repeats; process startup and input parsing are excluded. ksw2 completed 1,991 of the 2,000 MinION pairs; the 9 missing pairs are excluded from the ratios. The artifact's ksw2 wrapper passes the raw ASCII sequences rather than the 0-3 encoded copies it builds; ksw2's fast path only compares bases for equality, and the scores match WFA2 on all 3,317 pairs, so results are correct. The memory_kb column looked inconsistent and was not used. Edlib (edit distance only, not gap-affine) is faster than every WFA2 mode in this data, and BitPAl's score-only mode is about as fast as WFA2 high-memory (7.5x vs ksw2). The speedup is algorithmic (wavefront O(ns) versus full O(n^2) DP) rather than from SIMD intrinsics, so the simd-intrinsics-libraries category is a loose fit.

notes: Confirmed at B. Ratios re-derived from statistics_all.tsv.gz: wfa-high vs ksw2-extz2-sse 7.26x total (median 12.2x, faster on 98.6% of pairs) on 1,326 ONT-region pairs and 7.51x (median 4.6x) on 1,991 MinION pairs; BiWFA 9.95x and 9.76x; scores agree on all 3,317 pairs. Shortcomings: CPU model unstated, measured code is a 2022 paper snapshot, favourable low-divergence long-read workload, edlib (edit distance only) faster than all WFA2 modes; a paper-access retier could reach A if the paper names the CPU.

tier_reason: First-party raw Catch timing dumps (experiments/results/matmul/square_matmul_results.txt, experiments/results/timing/mcq_D=128_M=16.txt) from the repo's own cpp/test/quantize/profile_bolt.cpp, with no CPU model and no compiler flags (experiments/README only says Clang on OS X via Xcode). The KDD 2017 paper was unreachable (arXiv and ar5iv blocked); its abstract (snippet only) claims faster-than-BLAS matrix multiply even counting compression, so a paper-access retier could move it to B.

corrections.caveats: First-party raw timing outputs with no CPU model and no compiler flags, so tier C even though a peer-reviewed KDD 2017 paper exists (arXiv, ar5iv and the ACM copy were not reachable; a search snippet of the abstract says approximate dot products can multiply matrices faster than a state-of-the-art BLAS even counting compression time, and gives distance and dot-product speedups up to 10x; the paper's hardware and baselines were not verified). The comparison is not the same computation: Bolt returns an approximate, quantized uint16 product built from 4-bit codes and 8-bit lookup tables, while the baseline is an exact float32 Eigen GEMM (`out.noalias() = X * Q`; single- or multi-threaded not stated, though the README's Xcode/Apple Clang build suggests single-threaded). The Bolt matmul rows use random codes, random centroids and random offsets (cpp/test/quantize/profile_bolt.cpp) and measure speed only; approximation quality is evaluated separately in Python. In that profile the helper _run_bolt_matmul takes the centroid, code, LUT and output matrices by value, so each timed call copies them (a cost charged to Bolt, up to a 134 MB output copy at N = 8192) and writes the product into the copy. The checked-in square_matmul test now enables only N = 64, 128 and 256 (the larger sizes are commented out), so the 512-8192 rows come from an earlier configuration. The 'PQ' and 'OPQ' baselines are the repo's own implementations, not FAISS, and the timing files contain no PQ scan row, so the slides' 10x-vs-PQ scan claim could not be reproduced from the files; only the encoding and lookup-table rows could. The Python README example says '~10x here' for numpy dot products, not C++ numbers. AVX2 required; the README says the Python wrapper no longer builds for many people. Last commit 2022-06-24.

notes: Confirmed at C; all medians in claimed_speedup re-derived from the result files (Eigen 13,190 ms vs Bolt<8> 231 ms at N = 8192, 57x; encode 39.8 ms PQ vs 2.29 ms Bolt; LUT 34.7 vs 1.42 ms). Shortcomings: approximate quantized output against exact float GEMM, self-implemented PQ baselines, no CPU or flags, random codes, abandoned since 2022; paper-access retier (KDD 2017, arXiv 1706.10283) could reach B.

tier_reason: First-party README Performance Analysis table against parasail and ksw2's own scalar DP; the test data and cli.c harness are in the repo and the Makefile shows default flags, but the table names no CPU, compiler or flags used. The minimap2 paper's ~3x-vs-parasail statement was seen only as a search snippet (preprint wording), so no B.

corrections.caveats: No CPU model, compiler or flags are stated for the timing table, so tier C. The README itself says KSW2 is faster than parasail 'partly because' KSW2 uses one score for all matches and another for mismatches while parasail takes a generic matrix, so the comparison is not quite the same task. The parasail rows are 32-bit-lane variants (ps_nw_*_32), the widths that do not saturate on 50 kb sequences; ksw2's Suzuki-Kasahara difference formulation keeps 8-bit lanes, which is the source of its win. Rows differ in what they compute (score-only global vs extension with Z-drop; the parasail rows do not list `-s` but report no CIGAR), and only the global score-only rows (0.96 s SSE2, 0.84 s SSE4) beat parasail's best 2.2 s; the extension rows (3.0 s and 2.7 s) are slower than parasail's global row. Test data are checked in (test/ has MT-human.fa, MT-orang.fa, q1.fa, t1.fa and gzipped q2 and t2; which files are the 50k and 16.5k pairs was not confirmed) so the table can be rerun on your own CPU with `make parasail=prefix`. A search snippet of the minimap2 preprint says the implementation is about three times as fast as parasail's 4-way vectorization for global alignment (snippet only, not verified in the published paper). Last commit 2023-06-27 (about 3.3 years ago); minimap2 carries its own copy of these sources. The Suzuki-Kasahara BMC Bioinformatics 2018 and minimap2 Bioinformatics 2018 papers were not opened (arXiv and publisher sites blocked).

notes: Confirmed at C; README table numbers match (0.84 s SSE4 extz2_sse -sg vs parasail ps_nw_striped_32 2.2 s, 2.6x derived; 8.7x vs scalar gg). Shortcomings: no CPU or compiler for the table, only the global score-only mode beats parasail, scoring model simpler than parasail's generic matrix, abandoned since 2023-06-27. Possible B via the minimap2 paper if a paper-access retier confirms the ~3x-vs-parasail sentence in the published version.
